summary: Defines the Memento framework, which lets users get past states of a web resource through datetime negotiation, a variation of content negotiation, and TimeMaps listing URIs of prior states. It is informational and works by extending HTTP.

plainLanguage.summary: A time machine for web pages: you say a date and get the old version.

questions: how to view old versions of a web page
how to access old versions of web pages
subtitle: Access past versions of web pages through datetime negotiation.

tldr.problem: Web resources change over time, but there is no standard way for a user to request an old version of a page, and archives that hold past versions are scattered and incompatible.
tldr.mechanism: Memento introduces datetime negotiation, where a user requests a specific date and the server returns the state the resource had at that time, plus links to TimeMaps that list available past versions. Servers use Accept-Datetime headers and Memento-Datetime responses to coordinate.
tldr.outcome: Users can now ask for and retrieve historical versions of web pages from archives, content management systems, or version control systems using a standardized approach that works across distributed systems.

facts.label: Primary use case
facts.value: Web archives, content management systems, version control

today: RFC 7089 is Informational and defines the Memento framework for accessing historical web content. Major web archives including the Internet Archive implement Memento, and it is used by libraries and digital preservation systems to provide standardized access to archived web resources.

sections.title: A Time Dimension for Web Resources
sections.content: Web resources change over time. A news site, a Wikipedia page, or a government document may be different today than it was a year ago. The Memento framework provides a way for users to access past states of web resources using standard HTTP interactions. It introduces datetime negotiation, which extends the familiar content negotiation mechanism (where you can request a specific media type or language) to the datetime dimension. Rather than asking for HTML or JSON, you can ask for the state of a page as it existed on a specific date.
sections.plainLanguage: The web is always changing. Memento lets you go back in time to see what a page looked like before.

sections.title: Core Concepts: Originals, Mementos, TimeGates, and TimeMaps
sections.content:
Memento introduces four concepts. An Original Resource is a resource that changes over time, like a web page. A Memento is a snapshot of an Original Resource at a point in the past. A TimeGate is a resource that accepts datetime negotiations and returns a Memento that best matches the requested date. A TimeMap is a list of all Mementos available for an Original Resource, with their archival dates.

These resources may reside on different servers. For example, the original page might be on example.com, while Mementos are in the Internet Archive (web.archive.org), and the TimeGate might be on yet another server. The framework is fully distributed: no single server needs to know about all versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Original is the live page. Memento is a saved copy from the past. TimeGate is what you ask to find a past copy. TimeMap lists all the copies available.

sections.title: HTTP Headers and Link Relations
sections.content:
Memento uses two new HTTP headers. The Accept-Datetime request header tells a TimeGate what date you want (formatted as RFC 1123 date, e.g., "Tue, 20 Mar 2001 20:35:00 GMT"). The Memento-Datetime response header tells you the actual date of the Memento returned (which may differ from your request if no exact match exists).

The framework defines four link relation types, expressed in HTTP Link headers. The original link points from a TimeGate or Memento to its Original Resource. The timegate link points from an Original Resource to its TimeGate. The timemap link points to the TimeMap listing all available Mementos. The memento link points to individual Mementos and includes a datetime attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Headers let the user say "I want the version from March 2001" and the server say "Here is the version from March 20, 2001 at 1:36 PM". Links connect the original page to the time machine, the time machine to its list of saved versions, and back again.

sections.title: Datetime Negotiation in Action
sections.content:
A user agent requests an Original Resource with an Accept-Datetime header specifying a desired date. The Original Resource responds with a Link header pointing to a TimeGate. The user agent then requests the TimeGate with the same Accept-Datetime. The TimeGate uses an algorithm (e.g., nearest-in-time or nearest-in-the-past) to select the best matching Memento and responds with a Location header pointing to it, plus a Link header pointing to the Original Resource and TimeMap. The user agent retrieves the Memento, which includes a Memento-Datetime header showing the actual date of that snapshot and links back to the Original Resource, TimeGate, and TimeMap.

The framework supports multiple implementation patterns. The Original Resource can act as its own TimeGate, a remote resource can act as the TimeGate, or Mementos can be provided without a TimeGate. Servers can use HTTP 302 redirects or 200 responses to deliver Mementos.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the live page "Do you have an old version?" It says "Ask my time machine." You ask the time machine for March 2001. It says "Here, follow this link to the snapshot." You get the old page with a date stamp.

sections.title: TimeMaps and Distributed Archives
sections.content:
A TimeMap is a resource that lists all Mementos available for an Original Resource. It typically serializes as a link-format list (RFC 5988) that includes each Memento with its archival datetime and optional links to successor or predecessor versions. A TimeMap may be incomplete or partial; it represents only the Mementos the responding server knows about. Multiple TimeGates and TimeMaps can exist for the same Original Resource, each maintained by different archives or services.

The framework is extensible. Regular content negotiation (requesting HTML vs. JSON) still works alongside datetime negotiation. Servers can provide "memento" links to related Mementos that match other content preferences (e.g., different languages or media types from nearby dates). Links may include license attributes to associate usage rights with archived snapshots.
sections.plainLanguage: A TimeMap is a catalog of all saved versions with their dates. Different archives can each maintain their own catalog. You can ask for an old version in HTML or PDF; the system will try to find one near your requested date.
